rub.e: From Middle English rubben, of unknown origin; possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rubbōną, a hypothetical variant of *ruppōną (“to tear (off), rip; to wear away, rub”), related to *reufaną (“to tear”) (> English reave). If so, a doublet of rip.

rubbing.e: From Middle English rubbinge, rubbynge, equivalent to rub + -ing.
rubbing.g: An impression of an embossed or incised surface made by placing a piece of paper over it and rubbing with graphite, crayon or other coloring

rubbish.e: From Middle English robous (“rubbish, building rubble”), further origin uncertain; possibly from Anglo-Norman rubous, rubouse, rubbouse (“refuse, waste material.

rubble.e: From Middle English rouble, rubel, robel, robeil, from Anglo-Norman *robel (“bits of broken stone”). Presumably related to rubbish, originally of same meaning (waste material, bits of stone, rubble). Ultimately presumably from Old Norse rubba (“to huddle, crowd together, heap up", possibly also "to rub, scrape”).
rubble.g: The broken remains of an object, usually rock or masonry.

ruby.e: From Middle English ruby, rube, from Old French rubi, from Medieval Latin rubīnus. Etymology 1 sense 7 (“pronunciation guide”) is from the British 5½-point type size (etymology 1 sense 6), used for annotations in printed documents.
ruby.g: A clear, deep, red variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.

rudder.e: From Middle English rodder, rother, ruder, from Old English rōþor (“oar, rudder”), from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr, from Proto-Germanic *rōþrą (“oar, rudder”).
rudder.g: An underwater vane used to steer a vessel. The rudder is controlled by means of a wheel, tiller or other apparatus (modern vessels can be co

ruddy.e: From Middle English rody, from Old English rudiġ (“reddish; ruddy”), from rudu + -iġ. By surface analysis, rud (“redness”) + -y. The British slang sense expressing irritation is presumably a euphemism for bloody.
ruddy.g: Reddish in color, especially of the face, fire, or sky.

rude.e: From Middle English rude, from Old French rude, ruide, from Latin rudis (“rough, raw, rude, wild, untilled”).
rude.g: Lacking in refinement or civility; bad-mannered; discourteous.

rudiment.e: From Old French rudiment, from Latin rudimentum (“a first attempt, a beginning”), plural rudimenta (“the elements”), from rudis (“rude”); see rude. By surface analysis, rude + -i- + -ment.
rudiment.g: A fundamental principle or skill, especially in a field of learning.

rue.e: From Middle English rewe, reowe, from Old English hrēow (“sorrow, regret, penitence, repentance, penance”), from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwu (“pain, sadness, regret, repentance”). Probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *krows-.

From Middle English rewen, ruwen, ruen, reowen, from Old English hrēowan (“to rue; make sorry; grieve”), perhaps influenced by Old Norse hryggja (“to distress, grieve”), from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną (“to sadden; repent”).
rue.g: To repent of or regret (some past action or event); to wish that a past action or event had not taken place.

rug.e: Uncertain; probably of North Germanic origin; perhaps inherited via Middle English *rugge (suggested by Middle English ruggy (“hairy, shaggy, bristly”) and rugged (“hairy, shaggy, rugged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“shagginess, tuft”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwō (“long wool”), probably related to *rūhaz (“rough”), related to English rag and rough.
rug.g: A partial covering for a floor.

ruin.e: From Middle English ruyne, ruine, from Old French ruine, from Latin ruīna (“overthrow, ruin”), from ruō (“to fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush”).
ruin.g: The remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction, such as a house or castle.

ruinous.e: From Middle English ruynous, from Old French ruinos, ruineus, from Latin ruīnōsus. By surface analysis, ruin + -ous.

rule.e: From Middle English reule, rewle, rule, borrowed from Old French riule, reule, from Latin regula (“straight stick, bar, ruler, pattern”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”), from the root *h₃reǵ-; see regent.
From Middle English reulen, rulen, borrowed from Old French riuler, from Latin regulāre (“to regulate, rule”), from regula (“a rule”); see regular and regulate.
rule.g: To regulate, be in charge of, make decisions for, reign over.

ruler.e: From Middle English reuler; equivalent to rule + -er.
ruler.g: A (usually rigid), flat, rectangular measuring or drawing device with graduations in units of measurement; a straightedge with markings.

ruling.g: That rules; predominant; chief; reigning; controlling.

rumble.e: From Middle English rumblen, romblen, rummelyn, frequentative form of romen (“to roar”), equivalent to rome + -le.
rumble.g: A low, heavy, continuous sound, such as that of thunder or a hungry stomach.

rumor.e: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumeur, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewH- (“to shout, to roar”).
rumor.g: A statement or claim of questionable accuracy, from no known reliable source, usually spread by word of mouth.

rumour.e: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumour, rumor, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewH- (“to shout, roar”).
rumour.g: UK, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, and Ireland spelling of rumor.

rump.e: From Middle English rumpe, from Old Norse rumpr (“rump”), from Middle Low German rump (“the bulk or trunk of a body, trunk of a tree”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rumpō (“trunk of a tree, log”). The ultimate origin could be related to Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”) (Dutch rimpel and German rümpfen (“to wrinkle”)).
rump.g: The hindquarters of a four-legged mammal, not including its legs

run.e: From Middle English runnen, rennen (“to run”), alteration (due to the past participle runne, runnen, yronne) of Middle English rinnen (“to run”), from Old English rinnan, iernan (“to run”) and Old Norse rinna (“to run”), both from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to boil, churn”).

runner.e: From Middle English rennere, rynner, urnare, equivalent to run + -er.
runner.g: Agent noun of run; one who runs.

running.g: Moving or advancing at a run.

runs.e: Usually said to allude to the fact that an affected person is frequently running to get to a toilet immediately. Sometimes said to allude to the runniness (runny consistency) of the stool.

rural.e: From Old French rural, from Latin rūrālis (“rural”), from rūs (“countryside”) + -ālis.
rural.g: Relating to the countryside or to agriculture.

rush.e: Perhaps from Middle English ruschen, russchen (“to rush, startle, make a loud rushing noise”), from Old English hrysċan (“to jolt, startle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hurskijan, from Proto-Germanic *hurskijaną (“to startle, drive”), from *hurskaz (“fast, rapid, quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run, hurry”).

From Middle English risshe, rusch, risch, from Old English rysċ, rysċe, risċ, risċe, from a merger of Proto-West Germanic *riskijā, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)resg- (“to weave”) and Proto-West Germanic *ruskijā, possibly borrowed from Latin rūscum (“butcher's broom”), of unknown origin + *-jā (animal and plant suffix).
rush.g: Any of several stiff plants of the genus Juncus, or the family Juncaceae, having hollow or pithy stems and small flowers, and often growing

rust.e: From Middle English rust, rost, roust, from Old English rust, rūst (“rust”), from Proto-West Germanic *rust, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz (“rust”), from Proto-Indo-European *rudʰso- (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”).
rust.g: The deteriorated state of iron or steel as a result of moisture and oxidation; it consists mostly of iron(III) oxide (ferric oxide) and iron

rust.e: From Middle English rusten, from the noun (see above).
rust.g: To oxidize, especially of iron or steel.

rut.e: From Middle English rutte (noun) and rutten (verb), from Old French rut (“noise, roar, bellowing”), from Latin rugītus, from rugīre (“to roar”).
rut.g: Sexual desire in any of many mammals, often specific to mating season; the state or season in which this is experienced.

rut.e: Origin uncertain. Possibly from Middle English route, from Middle French route (“road”), from Old French route. Alternatively, possibly an alteration of rit (“groove, furrow”), from Middle English ritten (“to score, scratch, cut, tear open”).
rut.g: A furrow, groove, or track worn in the ground, as from the passage of many wheels along a road.

ruthless.e: From Middle English reuþeles; equivalent to ruth + -less.
ruthless.g: Without pity or compassion; cruel, pitiless.
